summary: Presents a technique to securely provision a networking device that boots in a factory-default state. It can update the boot image, commit an initial configuration, and run scripts, and it works on both public and private networks. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A new router in a box has to learn its settings. This is a safe way for it to get them as soon as it is plugged in, and to check that the instructions are really from its owner.

questions: how does zero touch provisioning work
subtitle: How a factory-fresh network device finds its boot image and configuration on its own, and proves the instructions are genuine.

tldr.problem: Sending trained specialists to every site to install devices is too costly and does not scale, yet a device booting in its factory-default state has no reason to trust whatever data it finds.
tldr.mechanism: The device checks a list of bootstrapping data sources (removable storage, DNS, DHCP, bootstrap servers) and accepts onboarding information only from a trusted server or when it is signed by the owner, backed by a manufacturer-signed ownership voucher.
tldr.outcome: Non-technical staff only plug in power and network cables, and the device updates its boot image, commits an initial configuration and runs scripts. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9646.

facts.label: Redirect limit
facts.value: SHOULD be no more than ten

today: RFC 8572 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9646; it has not been obsoleted. Anyone implementing SZTP should read the update alongside it.

sections.title: Zero Touch Provisioning, Securely
sections.content:
RFC 8572 defines Secure Zero Touch Provisioning (SZTP), a bootstrapping strategy that lets devices securely obtain bootstrapping data with no installer action beyond physical placement and connecting network and power cables. Non-technical personnel can bring up devices in remote locations without any operator input.

The process can update the boot image, commit an initial configuration and execute arbitrary scripts. Afterwards the device can set up secure connections with other systems, for instance NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040) connections to a network management system (NMS).

The document mainly covers physical devices, whose initial state is set during manufacturing. It names two use cases: a device attached to a remotely administered network, such as a branch office, which must reach an Internet-based bootstrap server, and a device on a locally administered network, which may also use nearby devices to find a local service.
sections.eli5: Imagine a new game console that sets itself up the moment you plug it in, and only listens to instructions that really came from its owner.

sections.title: Redirect and Onboarding Information
sections.content:
A device can receive two kinds of conveyed information. Redirect information points the device at other bootstrap servers: a list where each entry has a hostname or IP address, an optional port and an optional trust anchor certificate used to authenticate that server.

Onboarding information carries what the device needs to set itself up: details of the boot image it must run, an initial configuration to commit, and scripts to execute (a pre-configuration script and a post-configuration script).

Either kind is trusted if it arrives over a secure connection to a trusted bootstrap server or is signed by the device's owner. Otherwise it is untrusted. Untrusted redirect information is still useful, because it can send a device to a server where signed data is waiting, but the device then discards any trust anchors it contains. Onboarding information must be trusted to be of any use; there is no option to process untrusted onboarding information.
sections.eli5: A redirect is a note saying 'go ask at that desk'. Onboarding is the actual setup instructions. The device only follows setup instructions if it can tell they are genuine.

sections.title: The Three Artifacts
sections.content:
Bootstrapping data is made of three artifacts, each wrapped in a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) structure.

  • Conveyed information: the redirect or onboarding information itself, which may be unsigned, signed, encrypted, or signed and then encrypted.
  • Owner certificate: an X.509 certificate identifying the owner, used to verify the signature on the conveyed information. It MUST include the intermediate certificates up to the pinned-domain-cert from the voucher, and MAY carry fresh revocation objects such as CRLs and OCSP responses.
  • Ownership voucher: signed by the device's manufacturer, it securely identifies the device's owner and is used to verify the owner certificate. Its format comes from RFC 8366.

Any artifact MAY be encrypted, using a CMS EnvelopedData wrapper and the device's secure identity certificate. Data is always signed first and then encrypted, never the reverse. That hides the signer's certificate and lets an owner inspect an unencrypted voucher and encrypt it later.

Only three groupings make sense: unsigned data (no voucher or owner certificate), signed data without revocations, and signed data with revocations.
sections.eli5: Think of a sealed letter (the instructions), a signature card from the owner, and a note from the toy factory saying 'this owner really owns this toy'. Together they prove the letter is real.

sections.title: Sources of Bootstrapping Data
sections.content:
The RFC defines four sources and says the list is not exhaustive. Each maps the three artifacts onto its own medium.

  • Removable storage (such as a USB flash drive): needs no external infrastructure, and the boot image can sit on the same drive. It is untrusted, so data must be signed or processable provisionally.
  • DNS server: device-specific TXT records under <serial-number>._sztp carry the artifacts in keys ci, oc and ov. Device-independent SRV records under _sztp._tcp carry unsigned redirect information. Signed data is large by DNS standards, so DNS over TCP is expected to be needed.
  • DHCP server: DHCP can convey so little data that only unsigned redirect information fits.
  • Bootstrap server: a RESTCONF server with the YANG module from the RFC. It may be trusted or untrusted, and it also accepts progress reports from the device.

A bootstrap server has only two endpoints, one for the get-bootstrapping-data RPC and one for report-progress. The device sends optional inputs such as signed-data-preferred, hw-model, os-name, os-version and nonce, and receives the artifacts, plus a reporting-level for onboarding servers.
sections.eli5: A device can look for its instructions in four places: a USB stick, the phone book (DNS), the network's front desk (DHCP), or a special help server. Some places are safer than others, so the device checks signatures.

sections.title: What the Device Does
sections.content:
A device must start with a flag enabling SZTP set to true, and with read-only trust anchors, a list of well-known bootstrap servers and a protected private key. On power-up, if SZTP is configured it tries each supported source in turn. If none works it loops back and tries again; if one works it runs with the new configuration.

Processing is a recursive algorithm built on a trust-state variable that starts FALSE. It becomes TRUE when the device authenticates a bootstrap server against a trust anchor, or when it validates signed data. A successful run is zero or more redirects followed by one onboarding response. Implementations MUST limit recursive redirects, and the limit SHOULD be no more than ten. If onboarding information arrives while trust-state is FALSE, the device MUST abandon it.

To validate signed data, the device first authenticates the voucher against its pre-configured trust anchors and checks its serial number and dates (if the clock is accurate). Then it verifies the owner certificate against the voucher's pinned-domain-cert, and finally checks that the conveyed information was signed by that owner certificate. If any step fails, the signed data is invalid.

Onboarding information is processed in a fixed order: boot image (download, verify, install, then reboot), pre-configuration script, atomic commit of the initial configuration, post-configuration script. Any error stops the process and returns the device to the bootstrapping sequence. When talking to a trusted server, the device sends progress reports such as bootstrap-initiated and bootstrap-complete; to an untrusted server it MUST NOT send any.
sections.eli5: The device is a careful kid. It checks each possible source, asks 'can I prove this is real?', and only follows the setup steps in order if the answer is yes. If anything goes wrong it stops and tries somewhere else.

sections.title: The DHCP Redirect Options
sections.content:
Two DHCP options deliver a list of bootstrap server URIs. They are semantically the same but syntactically different: OPTION_V4_SZTP_REDIRECT (option code 143) for DHCPv4 and OPTION_V6_SZTP_REDIRECT (option code 136) for DHCPv6.

Each URI entry is a 2-octet uri-length followed by the URI, which MUST use the https scheme in the form https://<ip-address-or-hostname>[:<port>]. Clients ignore invalid entries, and MUST discard an option with no valid entry.

Because a DHCPv4 option is limited to 255 octets, a long list is split across several instances following RFC 3396. The DHCPv6 option is a singleton, so servers MUST NOT send more than one instance. The options cannot carry a trust anchor, since the redirect is unsigned and the device would discard it anyway.
sections.eli5: The network's front desk can hand the device a short list of web addresses to try. The list is only a hint, not a promise, so the device still has to check what it finds there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC spends many pages on risks. The key ones are below.

  • Clocks. Certificates and vouchers need an accurate clock. Implementations SHOULD NOT rely on NTP, and if clock accuracy cannot be ensured they are told to disable the clock-sensitive checks.
  • Blind connections. A device may accept an unknown server's TLS certificate to follow untrusted redirects. To compensate, data from an untrusted server must be signed.
  • Disclosure. Devices should be cautious with untrusted servers, since a client certificate reveals at least the serial number. They use get-bootstrapping-data but not report-progress, and SHOULD NOT send a secret such as a password through HTTP authentication.
  • Manufacturer reliance. Control shifts toward manufacturers, who maintain the well-known bootstrap servers and voucher-signing authorities. Operators can block the servers with an external firewall but cannot stop vouchers being generated.
  • Compromise. A compromised trusted server could return unsigned data of any sort, and a trusted redirect can cascade: compromise of one interaction may compromise all later ones.
  • Keys and validity. Trust anchors must be protected from modification and long-lived private keys stored in something like a TPM. Conveyed information has no validity period of its own, so a unique owner certificate per signed artifact is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The biggest worries are a wrong clock, a stranger pretending to be the owner, and trusting the toy maker too much. The device guards against them by checking signatures and keeping its secrets safe.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered several things for SZTP: the two YANG modules, two CMS content types (id-ct-sztpConveyedInfoXML and id-ct-sztpConveyedInfoJSON), DHCPv4 option 143 and DHCPv6 option 136.

It also registered the service name sztp for TCP, used to build the SRV label _sztp, with the note that the protocol uses HTTPS as a substrate, and the TXT node name _sztp in the underscored DNS node names registry.
sections.eli5: The authors reserved a few official names and numbers so nobody else would use them for something different.
